I didn't really make myself clear enough, or, at least, I didn't answer your initial question. My answer to your initial question should make things clearer.

You asked "Why are atheists so insistent that science and religion are incompatible?" My answer is that science is evidence-based, while religion values belief more than evidence.

Now before I go any further, let me take a moment to specify what I mean by "seriously religious", because I've used this phrase before and will use it again. A "seriously religious" person is someone who genuinely believes, or tries to genuinely believe, that there are such things as gods and that they do have a real influence on the world. I don't have a problem with people who just follow a particular set of rituals (going to church, burning incense in front of a shrine to their ancestors, etc.) simply because it's traditional in their family, so long as they don't actually believe that their god/ancestors exists/can actually hear them. Nor do I have a problem with someone who simply goes to church so as to fit in with the local culture or because they believe that there are social or psychological benefits from performance of group rituals. Where I have a problem is with people who actually believe this stuff. I have a problem with people who actually believe something that is false. By any reasonable standard of evidence we can say with complete confidence that there are no gods, there is no karma, and there is no life beyond this one. If someone believes there is, or aspires to believe there is, I can't take them seriously intellectually, because they are believing a falsity.

The problem with the seriously religious and the sciences is that science relies on positive evidence: scientists aim to believe only in true statements. I'm actually an economist myself, so I'm not a hardcore scientist, but I'd like to think that economics (at least as I practise it and teach it) is about making true statements and not believing falsities. If the sky is blue, I desire to believe that the sky is blue; if the sky is not blue, I desire to believe that the sky is not blue. If there are gods, I desire to believe that there are gods; if there are no gods, I desire to believe that there are no gods. Under any reasonable evidence-based belief system there are no gods, therefore I desire to believe that there are no gods.

The problem with the seriously religious is that they desire to believe a falsity. My problem with this from a professional point of view is that if they are prepared to believe that something false is true in one area, I cannot be confident that they will not make the same mistake in their professional activities. I couldn't advise someone whose commitment to truth is in doubt; I want my PhD candidates to be committed to the truth above all else.

My problem with the seriously religious from a personal point of view is the same: they want to believe a falsity. Most of the time I don't care what people believe - I think religious belief is fine for the 80% or more of the population who don't have anything interesting or useful to say or contribute, and religion is a great comfort to many fluffy-minded people. No. Science is able to provide a full account of the universe without requiring any additional invisible components. You, on the other hand, have to prove not just that there is an invisible component, but also that your particular invisible component (whichever god or gods you espouse) is the particular one that provides a correct explanation. That is, you must not only prove that your god exists, you must also prove that all the other possible religious explanations are false.

Your other points: a "rational Christian" who believes in some sort of personalisation of "the catalyst that sparked the Big Bang" has entirely misunderstood the physics of the Big Bang; someone who conceives of a god as "the 'entity' behind it all when things repeatedly go our way" has entirely misunderstood probability theory (and on this one I can speak with substantial professional confidence!); a conception of god as "the reason love exists" has misunderstood the biology of reproduction and social behaviour; and so on.

As for "agnostics", I have very little time for them. Of course in normal social discourse any civilised person (atheist or religious) will describe themselves as agnostic, so as to avoid pointless disagreements - I do it myself all the time, and so do most people - but my own view is that if someone describes themselves as agnostic in a serious discussion of religion they're being as intellectually dishonest with themselves as the seriously religious are: by any reasonable standards the only possible conclusion is that there is no god/karma/afterlife/whatever, and to fail to accept this is an act of intellectual cowardice.
